deck.title: From a physics model to a computational experiment
deck.visual_contract: Each slide is a single ImageGen-generated raster image embedded full-slide.
deck.delivery_context: 120-minute Week 1 teaching deck; timing appears only in speaker notes and package metadata, never in student-facing slide content.
deck.branding_override: No branding, logo, watermark, URL, footer, or institutional mark is permitted.
deck.canvas: 16:9 pure white canvas; no outer border or frame; no mesh, network, molecular, corner, texture, gradient, or background decoration; locked Roboto Condensed Bold navy title and Roboto Medium charcoal subtitle at the same upper-left anchor on every slide

slides.title: From a physics model to a computational experiment
slides.subtitle: Week 1 | Programming fundamentals through radioactive decay
visual_text: A sample has a half-life of 6.0 h.
How should we simulate one day — and decide whether the answer deserves trust?

notes.checkpoint: Ask students to predict the fraction remaining after one and four half-lives before showing any code.
notes.transition: Use the question to frame the lecture arc: MATLAB is the instrument, not the physics model.

slides.title: Today’s arc: ask → compute → test
slides.subtitle: A physics question becomes a numerical experiment
visual_text: Map physical quantities to variables and units
Compare with a reference and justify dt
Record evidence so another person can rerun it
Course roadmap: Week 1 foundations → later numerical methods

notes.checkpoint: Which stage would be missing if we only showed a final plot?
notes.transition: Make the cycle explicit before introducing the MATLAB interface.

slides.title: Computation is a controlled experiment on a model
slides.subtitle: Every arrow carries a decision that should remain visible.
visual_text: A graph alone is not evidence.

notes.checkpoint: Have students name one quantity that belongs to the physical model and one that belongs to the numerical method.
notes.transition: Now locate the minimum MATLAB views needed to carry the cycle out.

slides.title: Four MATLAB views, one repeatable experiment
slides.subtitle: Know where to try, save, inspect, and rerun your work.
visual_text: Try one expression and inspect its answer.
Save the sequence of choices: text + code + output.
Inspect variables currently in memory — useful, but easy to treat as hidden input.
Keep the script and related files together.
Use the Editor / Live Editor for work you intend to rerun.

notes.checkpoint: Ask: where should the experiment live if a classmate must rerun it tomorrow?
notes.transition: The next step is naming quantities so the code carries units and assumptions with it.

slides.title: Readable names make units and assumptions visible
slides.subtitle: The syntax is small; the naming discipline is the habit.
visual_text: Use = to store a value in a named variable.
Use arithmetic to translate an expression.
Use % to explain a choice to the next reader.
A suffix such as _h or _m2 keeps dimensions visible.
Unit check: lambda_per_h × dt_h must be dimensionless.

notes.checkpoint: What unit does lambda_per_h carry? What unit must dt_h carry?
notes.transition: Use the same naming habits in the physics-based Onramp diagnostic before the decay model.

slides.title: Onramp skills become evidence in a cooling experiment
slides.subtitle: Lab 01 diagnostic: build, inspect, and test a temperature model.
visual_text: Diagnostic habits: arrays | element-wise operations | indexing | plotting | validation
The code is short; the reasoning must remain visible.

notes.checkpoint: Before computing, ask students to predict the initial value, the long-time limit, and whether the model can cross below room temperature.
notes.transition: The diagnostic uses familiar Onramp operations as evidence; the lecture now applies the same reasoning chain to radioactive decay.

slides.title: Start with a prediction, then write the model
slides.subtitle: A closed sample with a constant half-life gives a controlled physical question.
visual_text: A sample has half-life 6.0 h. How many undecayed nuclei remain after 24 h?
same decay probability per unit time
A physical population should not become negative.

notes.checkpoint: Collect predictions: what should remain after one half-life and four half-lives?
notes.transition: Translate the symbols into names that MATLAB can store without hiding the units.

slides.title: Map physics symbols to readable MATLAB names
slides.subtitle: A parameter map prevents notation and units from drifting during coding.
visual_text: Dimension check: lambda_per_h × dt_h is dimensionless.

notes.checkpoint: Ask students to explain why lambda_per_h and dt_h must use the same time unit.
notes.transition: With the parameters named, construct the exact reference before approximating it.

slides.title: The exact solution is a reference, not a shortcut
slides.subtitle: Use the benchmark to make approximation error visible.
visual_text: Prediction before computing: what should the numerical curve approach?
A benchmark does not remove the need for numerical work; it gives the work something to answer to.

notes.checkpoint: Ask students to read the reference value at 24 h and state its physical meaning.
notes.transition: Now replace continuous time with an aligned array of discrete times.

slides.title: Build the time array before the loop
slides.subtitle: One time value must align with one stored population value.
visual_text: N(1) is N0 because MATLAB indexing starts at 1.
t_h(2) = dt_h ↔ N(2) after one update
Common trap: N(0) is not a MATLAB index.

notes.checkpoint: Point to the first two entries and ask which value is known before the loop runs.
notes.transition: The derivative approximation supplies the rule that fills the next entry.

slides.title: Turn the derivative into a next-value rule
slides.subtitle: Forward Euler keeps the model but approximates the time derivative.
visual_text: 1  Start with the model:  dN/dt = -lambda N
This is not the exact physics; it is a discrete method for carrying the model forward.
Warning: if lambda dt > 1, the factor can become negative.

notes.checkpoint: Have students identify which term must be dimensionless in the update factor.
notes.transition: Write the same three-step logic as a minimal MATLAB loop.

slides.title: The loop is the algorithm written out
slides.subtitle: Read it as current value → update rule → next value.
visual_text: 2  Multiply by the dimensionless factor 1 - lambda_per_h*dt_h
3  Store the new value in N(n+1)
Overwrite N(n) instead of writing N(n+1)
Loop to numel(t_h) and write past the end
Forget N(1) = N0 before the loop
Checkpoint: what does one pass through the loop represent physically?

notes.checkpoint: Trace one iteration on the board: which stored value is read, changed, and preserved?
notes.transition: The code is ready; design a fair numerical experiment by changing only dt.

slides.title: Hold the physics fixed; vary one numerical choice
slides.subtitle: A fair timestep experiment changes resolution while keeping the model the same.
visual_text: Same update rule; different number of steps
Cost is part of the result.

notes.checkpoint: Ask which quantities must not change when comparing timesteps.
notes.transition: Plot the four approximations against the same exact reference.

slides.title: Coarse and fine Euler curves separate from the reference
slides.subtitle: The visual comparison shows why resolution is a modelling decision.
visual_text: Coarse Euler steps fall below the exact curve at 24 h.
Fine steps track the reference more closely.
Question: which curve would you report first — and what evidence would you add?

notes.checkpoint: Have students rank the curves before revealing the table of final errors.
notes.transition: Convert the visual impression into a numerical error and cost report.

slides.title: Smaller dt improves the result — at a measurable cost
slides.subtitle: Approved checkpoints for T_half_h = 6.0 h and tMax_h = 24 h
visual_text: dt (h) | lambda*dt | Euler N/N0 at 24 h | relative error | steps
Trend: smaller dt → lower error, more steps
A numerical result includes accuracy and cost.

notes.checkpoint: Ask students to choose a timestep for a first report and defend it using error plus cost.
notes.transition: A trustworthy report also needs checks on physics, units, implementation, and communication.

slides.title: Trust comes from a trail of checks
slides.subtitle: Validation is evidence that the implementation and interpretation agree with a trusted check.
visual_text: lambda and t use the same time unit
Update rule, initial condition, index range
At least two timesteps and a relative error
Labels, units, legend, and one interpretation
Warning: lambda*dt > 1 can make the Euler population negative.

notes.checkpoint: Which assertion would catch a missing initial condition? Which would catch a nonphysical negative population?
notes.transition: Checks make the result defensible; reproducibility makes the checks portable to another person and another day.

slides.title: AI can suggest syntax; it cannot certify physics
slides.subtitle: Responsible AI use means verification literacy, not blind acceptance.
visual_text: 1 Read the code line by line
3 Compare with N_exact and report error
4 Rerun from a fresh MATLAB session
Whether the physical assumptions fit the sample
Whether lambda and dt use compatible units
Whether the chosen timestep is adequate for the question
parameters + units | dt + tMax | MATLAB version | validation evidence | labelled figure + caption
Checkpoint: what evidence makes your dt acceptable?

notes.checkpoint: Invite one student example of a test that an AI-generated answer would not perform automatically.
notes.transition: Close by turning the full cycle into a practical handoff and exit ticket.

slides.title: Leave with a model, a method, and a test you can rerun
slides.subtitle: The next task transfers the reasoning chain to a cooling model.
visual_text: A computational result begins with a model and assumptions — not with a MATLAB command.
dt is part of the numerical method. Smaller is not automatically free.
Validation and interpretation are required parts of a simulation.
Predict, compute, validate, and interpret the cooling model.
Exit ticket: model + assumption | algorithm | validation evidence

notes.checkpoint: Collect the three-sentence exit ticket before students leave.
notes.transition: End with the practical handoff: complete the entry check, then transfer the reasoning chain to the cooling-model Onramp diagnostic.
